https://www.barrons.com/articles/citizens-bank-stock-gets-two-upgrades-but-still-doesnt-rally-1540222382 Citizens Bank Stock Gets Two Upgrades, but Still Doesn’t Rally By Updated Oct. 22, 2018 11:37 a.m. ET Order Reprints Ty Wright/Bloomberg Text size
Only a truly unloved stock can receive a Barron’s recommendation and two Wall Street upgrades and erase all of the resulting gains by noon.
Citizens Financial Group (ticker: CFG) initially rose more than 2% in early trading on Monday, after two analysts raised their ratings: Bank of America Merrill Lynch (BAML) upgraded the shares to Buy from Underperform, and Macquarie raised its rating by one level to Neutral. Yet the stock was nearly flat at $36.36 by midmorning. (At least it outperformed the S&P 500’s 0.2% decline.) The company was also selling $300 million of preferred shares Monday, with yield expected around 6.375%, according to early price talk.
BAML’s upgrade comes just three days after a better-than-expected earnings report and a bullish piece from Barron’s , which drew attention to the steady growth in the regional bank’s portfolio of commercial and consumer loans. The Rhode Island-based bank’s loan growth has been fueled in part by a partnership with Apple (AAPL) to finance purchases of smartphones made directly from the manufacturer. TransferWise CEO Kristo Kaarmann talks to MarketWatch about how fintech is disrupting cross-border money transfers, allowing consumers to send funds at a cost that's up to 12 times cheaper than what banks would offer.
And thanks to the lack of lasting gains on Monday, the most compelling part of the case for Citizens Financial’s stock is still in place: The shares are extremely cheap.
Bank of America Merrill Lynch focuses on valuations in its upgrade note on Monday. BAML is forecasting that the regional bank will report earnings per share of $3.90 next year. Even including the “material discount” at which Citizens trades (11 times earnings) compared with its regional-bank peers (13 times earnings), Citizens should trade at $43 per share, 18% above its midmorning price.
So what’s responsible for the discount? Macquarie thinks the explanation can be found in its relatively high “deposit beta,” or the speed at which Citizens passes through interest-rate increases to investors after the Federal Reserve raises rates.
In other words, the regional bank is being punished for giving individual depositors higher returns on their cash than its peers, a practice that is seen as increasing costs. BAML says that four rate increases in the next year would hit earnings per share by less than 1%. Newsletter Sign-up
Even if we assume that such a hit justifies the discount assigned to Citizens’ shares, BAML points out that “the market is pricing in a cost of equity at CFG that is about 350bp greater than for arguably [the] most complex bank globally—JPM.”
If Citizens makes just $3.75 per share in earnings next year, and commands a share price that’s just 10 times those earnings—the S&P 500 trades at about 16 times next year’s forecast earnings—that means it should a fair value of $37.50, still above its current share price, says BAML.
If Citizens were valued at levels similar to its peers, it would command $51 per share, BAML says. That would be a 40% increase.
